questions.stem: During an overnight validation run for a pharmacy robot, the cart enters the final corridor at \(5.2\,\text{m/s}\) while its automatic braking system can provide a constant deceleration of only \(1.4\,\text{m/s}^2\). The robot is \(8.0\,\text{m}\) from a locked medication cabinet, and the supervising engineer wants a short written explanation instead of a bare number. Explain whether the robot stops before the cabinet and show how the relevant constant-acceleration relationship supports your conclusion.
questions.answer: Using \(v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2a\Delta x\) with \(v_f=0\), \(v_i=5.2\,\text{m/s}\), and \(a=-1.4\,\text{m/s}^2\), the stopping distance is \(\Delta x \approx 9.66\,\text{m}\). Because \(9.66\,\text{m} > 8.0\,\text{m}\), the robot would still be moving at the cabinet. The braking system alone is therefore not enough to stop it in time.

questions.stem: A compact research capsule is launched straight upward from the roof of a medical imaging center with an initial speed of \(20\,\text{m/s}\). Neglect air resistance unless a part states otherwise.

parts.stem: Determine the time required for the capsule to reach its maximum height.
parts.answer: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so \(0 = v_0 - gt\). With \(v_0 = 20\,\text{m/s}\) and \(g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\), the time is \(t = 20/9.8 \approx 2.04\,\text{s}\).

parts.stem: Which statement best describes the capsule's acceleration while it is in flight?

options.text: The acceleration is zero at the top because the velocity is zero there.
options.explanation: This confuses velocity with acceleration. Gravity still provides a downward acceleration even when the velocity momentarily becomes zero.

options.text: The acceleration is upward while the capsule rises and downward while it falls.
options.explanation: This incorrectly ties acceleration direction to motion direction. In ideal projectile motion the acceleration stays downward the whole time.

options.text: The acceleration is downward and approximately \(9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\) throughout the flight.
options.explanation: With air resistance neglected, gravity is the only significant force after launch. That keeps the acceleration essentially constant at \(-g\), or downward with magnitude \(9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\), throughout the motion.

options.text: The acceleration steadily decreases to zero as the capsule approaches the top.
options.explanation: Nothing in the idealized model causes the gravitational acceleration to fade near the top of the trajectory. The acceleration does not taper to zero.
